title: Render the shipped area classification into the adopter configuration reference
description:
The adopter configuration reference and the copyable example configuration obtain the managed, permanent, and issue-scoped area lists from the shipped classification by generation, so neither carries a hand-maintained second copy that can go stale.

## Background

The shipped development-area classification is declared once in the engine, as the scaffolding constant that repository initialization renders into the configuration table a new repository receives. Two adopter-facing files restate parts of it by hand: the configuration reference carries a fenced block reproducing all three lists verbatim, and the copyable example carries a deliberately reduced illustrative subset that says so in a comment. Nothing binds either to the constant. Both went stale during earlier work and blocked two reviews before they were repaired.

Only one route to the shipped values respects the boundary between shipped behaviour and this repository's own configuration. Initializing a throwaway repository in a temporary directory produces the table the shipped constant renders; reading the configuration this repository runs under would report its local policy, which merely happens to agree today and is documented as a repository-local choice rather than a binding.

The example file keeps its hand-authored character everywhere else. Only its area-classification table becomes generated, and its illustrative subset gives way to the table a fresh repository actually receives, so a reader copying the file starts from the shipped classification.

One property of this route is load-bearing and easy to miss. Initialization runs from the installed binary, so the values the generator obtains are the classification compiled into the binary in use, not the declaration at the current revision. If a contributor edits the declaration and runs the generator without reinstalling, the regions are written from the older compiled copy: they are stale and internally consistent, so rerunning the generator changes nothing and the staleness survives. The repository already knows when an installed binary predates the sources it is judging, but that knowledge cannot help here — it identifies a repository by resolving a revision in it, and initialization runs in a temporary directory that has no repository at all, so nothing is reported. The generator therefore has to make the check itself, against the repository it is writing into.

Silence is not evidence either way, which is why the check has to be positive rather than an absence of complaint. A binary built without injected provenance reports its build commit as unknown, and an unknown commit, an unresolvable head, or a commit outside the repository's history all resolve to the same not-applicable outcome as a binary that is genuinely current. A binary from an ordinary install is therefore indistinguishable from a fresh one unless currency is established rather than assumed.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A repository-local generator initializes a throwaway repository in a temporary directory and reads the area-classification table written there, leaving the working tree it runs in otherwise unchanged.
- [hard] REQ-02: The generator writes that table into a marked region in the adopter configuration reference and into a marked region in the copyable example configuration.
- [hard] REQ-03: Bytes outside the markers in both targets are preserved exactly, including surrounding prose, authored comments, and every other configuration table.
- [hard] REQ-04: Neither target retains a hand-maintained restatement of the managed, permanent, or issue-scoped area lists.
- [hard] REQ-05: A second generator run immediately after the first finds nothing to change.
- [hard] REQ-06: The generator reads no configuration belonging to this repository, so the values it writes come only from what initialization produces.
- [hard] REQ-07: The generator writes only once it has positively established, against the repository it writes into rather than against the throwaway directory, that the binary it reads the classification from carries provenance resolvable in that repository and does not predate that repository's sources. Provenance that is absent, unresolvable, or outside that repository's history is a refusal to write, never a pass.

## Notes

The reference's surrounding prose already explains what the table is and where its authority lives; that prose stays hand-authored and only the values become generated.

One route to the currency check is available and one is a trap. The available one asks the binary itself: invoked from inside the repository with the marker that puts it in gate-child mode, it reports its own refusal status when it predates that repository, and existing coverage pins that behaviour. Reimplementing the check instead — reading the binary's reported build provenance, comparing it against the repository head, and re-deriving in shell which paths count as build inputs — would create a second copy of the very inventory this work exists to bind to one authority.

planning.outcome: The two adopter configuration files carry the shipped area classification as a generated region rather than authored prose.

terminal.test_boundary: the generator's own scratch-directory run compared against the committed regions
terminal.worker_sized_reason: One generator script writes two marked regions that no other work in this container edits.

title: A mechanical freshness check for the generated shipped-policy regions
description:
A deterministic check reports a generated shipped-policy region that no longer matches what repository initialization produces, so the two adopter configuration files cannot drift from the shipped classification unnoticed.

## Background

Generating the area-classification tables removes the hand-maintained copies, but generation alone does not keep them current: a change to the shipped classification leaves the committed regions correct-looking and wrong until someone reruns the generator. The repository's deterministic documentation checks exist for exactly this class of defect and already carry a member that re-renders configured projections and reports a difference.

That family has settled conventions. Each member is one committed script that derives both sides of its comparison live from the tree so it encodes no product facts of its own; each reports pass, a genuine finding, or an environment failure through three distinct exit statuses, with an environment failure dominating a finding; each guards its prerequisites up front and names the missing tool. Members split into those taking a caller-supplied footprint and those whose targets are fixed by configuration. A freshness check for two named documents belongs to the second class. A separate self-test harness proves each member in both directions by seeding a defect, asserting a non-zero result, then asserting a clean tree passes; that harness never mutates the real repository.

The family's own description enumerates its members by name, which makes the description a hand-maintained list that goes stale the moment a member is added.

One failure mode needs stating because it is neither a prerequisite nor a command failure. The classification the check compares against is produced by the installed binary, so a binary predating the repository under check produces an authoritative-looking but outdated table. Treating that as a difference emits a finding for what is an environment problem; treating it as nothing-to-compare passes vacuously, which is the more dangerous outcome. No refusal status arrives to be translated, because the refusal identifies a repository by resolving a revision in it and the classification is produced in a temporary directory that has none. The check therefore assesses that condition itself, against the repository it is checking, and classifies it as an environment failure.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A committed check compares the generated regions in both adopter configuration files against freshly produced output and reports a difference as a finding.
- [hard] REQ-02: The check derives both sides of its comparison live, encoding no copy of the shipped classification.
- [hard] REQ-03: The check reports pass, finding, and environment failure through the three distinct statuses the family already uses, guards its prerequisites before doing work, and reports any failure to obtain a trustworthy classification — a binary that predates the repository under check, and equally one whose provenance cannot be resolved against that repository — as an environment failure, never as a finding and never as a pass.
- [hard] REQ-04: The check runs against the working tree without leaving it modified.
- [hard] REQ-05: The check runs as part of the family's fan-out, and its result reaches the aggregate outcome under the family's precedence rules.
- [hard] REQ-06: The self-test harness proves three cases: a clean tree passes, a seeded stale region is reported as a finding, and an untrustworthy classification is reported as an environment failure.
- [hard] REQ-07: The family's own description no longer enumerates its members by name, so adding a member cannot make it stale.

## Notes

The check needs the generator's output, so it either invokes the generator against a scratch copy of the tree or reproduces its inputs; either way it must not depend on a value stated in the check itself.

planning.outcome: A stale generated policy region in either adopter configuration file fails the mechanical documentation checks.

terminal.test_boundary: the checker self-test harness exercising its three outcomes
terminal.worker_sized_reason: One checker in the shape of the existing projection check, plus its self-test block.

title: Generate the repository plan-template declaration from the packaged contribution
description:
The planning-bracket template this repository declares becomes a generated region rendered from the packaged contribution that is its authority, so the repository copy is no longer hand-authored.

## Background

The planning-bracket template is declared twice: once inline in the packaged workflow manifest as a semantic contribution, and once in this repository's own template registry. The two match on structure — roles, types, gates, document paths, labels, internal edges, anchor edges, and transforms are identical after parsing — and differ in three description strings.

The packaged declaration is the shipped artifact and the repository declaration is a local consumer of it, which fixes the direction: the packaged contribution is the authority and the repository copy becomes generated from it. The packaged contribution is already exposed whole through the package's machine-readable inspection output, so no new surface is needed to read it.

Two properties of the existing registry file constrain the change. Its seven-line header sits outside the template block and survives untouched. Inside the block, a six-line explanation records why the container anchor carries a whole-repository validation gate rather than the per-issue one, citing the criterion and invariant that motivated it; no round trip through a serializer preserves in-block commentary or the file's column alignment, so that rationale has to move outside the generated region to survive.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The repository plan-template declaration is a marked generated region whose body is rendered from the packaged planning-bracket contribution.
- [hard] REQ-02: Rendering leaves every byte outside the markers unchanged, including the file header.
- [hard] REQ-03: The rationale for the container anchor's whole-repository validation gate survives, stated outside the generated region.
- [hard] REQ-04: The three description strings that differ today are equal afterwards, with the packaged text taken as authoritative.
- [hard] REQ-05: The template registry loads the regenerated file, and the plan template still applies to the container type it applies to today.
- [hard] REQ-06: A second rendering run immediately after the first finds nothing to change.

## Notes

Two further plan-template declarations exist as adopter-facing illustrations of different rulesets. Both restate this declaration's top-level description string verbatim, and one also restates its planning-node description. They illustrate authoring forms rather than this repository's workflow and stay hand-authored; this work does not touch them.

planning.outcome: The repository plan-template block is a region rendered from the packaged declaration.

terminal.test_boundary: the template registry's own load of the regenerated file
terminal.worker_sized_reason: One renderer and one region inside a forty-eight-line configuration file, with the header preserved around it.

title: Fail the suite when the two plan-template declarations disagree
description:
A change to either plan-template declaration without the corresponding change to the other fails the test suite, compared as two parsed declarations rather than against a written-down expectation.

## Background

Generation makes the two declarations equal at the moment it runs. It does not keep them equal: a hand edit to the repository copy, or a change to the packaged contribution without a regeneration, puts them back out of step, and nothing today reports that. The pair has drifted before precisely because nothing compared them — the byte-equality contract that covers the packaged file assets does not reach this one, because the packaged declaration is inline manifest data rather than an asset.

The comparison has to be between the two parsed values. A test carrying its own expectation of what the template contains would be a third copy of the same declaration, going stale on the next change to either — the defect this work exists to remove, reintroduced in the guard meant to prevent it. Both sides are already parseable by the crate: the registry loads the repository file, and the packaged contribution is a value inside the embedded package.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A test parses the repository declaration and the packaged declaration and fails when any field differs, description strings included.
- [hard] REQ-02: The comparison rests on the two parsed values, holding no expectation of its own about what either contains.
- [hard] REQ-03: An edit to either declaration alone fails the suite, in whichever of the two it is made.
- [hard] REQ-04: The failure names the field that differs, so the reader knows which declaration to regenerate.

## Notes

The guard holds whether or not the region was regenerated, so it reports a hand edit to the generated region as readily as a change to the authority.

planning.outcome: A difference between the parsed repository declaration and the parsed packaged declaration fails the suite.

terminal.test_boundary: an in-crate comparison of the two parsed declarations
terminal.worker_sized_reason: One comparison between two values the crate can already parse, with no file rewritten by it.

title: Seed the provenance fixture with the repository sources the package draws from
description:
The isolated repository the build-stability fixture seeds includes the packaged live sources that sit under the tracker data root, so a build inside that fixture can read every source the package is assembled from.

## Background

The build-stability fixture seeds a throwaway git repository from an inventory of this repository's tracked and untracked inputs, then cold-builds every test target inside it and rebuilds to observe what a metadata-only change invalidates. Its inventory filter bans whole categories outright: the tracker data root, git internals, other agents' worktrees, and generated trees.

One packaged asset lives under the tracker data root — the content standards reference the package installs for adopters. While the package carries its own checked-in copy, that ban is harmless. Once the packaged tree is assembled from the repository files it mirrors, a build inside the seeded fixture cannot find that source and the fixture's cold baseline build fails. The failure would surface as an unexplained build error in a suite about relinking, far from its cause.

The ban exists for a reason: seeding a fixture with a repository's issue data would make every issue mutation an input to a build-stability measurement. The exception has to be narrow enough to keep that property and explicit enough that a later reader does not widen it back to the whole root.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The seeded fixture repository contains the packaged sources that live under the tracker data root.
- [hard] REQ-02: The rest of the tracker data root stays out of the fixture, so issue data is still not a build-stability input.
- [hard] REQ-03: The filter states why the exception is narrow, in terms a later reader can apply rather than reverse.
- [hard] REQ-04: Git internals, other agents' worktrees, and generated trees stay banned.
- [hard] REQ-05: The seeded fixture's cold baseline build succeeds with the additional sources present.

## Notes

The exception is derived from what the package declares rather than named as a single file path where that is practical, so a second packaged source under the same root needs no further edit here.

planning.outcome: The provenance fixture repository carries the packaged live sources, so a cold build inside it succeeds.

terminal.test_boundary: the seeded-repository build stability suite
terminal.worker_sized_reason: One filter predicate narrows, with the rationale that keeps a later reader from widening it.

title: Give the executable-mode contract a guard of its own
description:
The executable declaration each packaged asset carries is checked against the actual mode of the repository file it is drawn from by an assertion that stands on its own, so the contract survives the removal of the comparison it currently shares a loop with.

## Background

Each packaged asset declares whether it should be published with the executable bit set; seven of the sixty-one do. One test checks that declaration against the real mode of the repository file the asset mirrors, in both directions, and it is the only place in the workspace that checks it at all. The embedding carries no mode metadata, so nothing else can recover the fact.

That check lives inside a loop whose other half compares the two copies of each asset byte for byte. The byte half is on its way out: once the packaged tree is produced by copying the repository files, comparing the copy to its source compares a thing to itself. When the byte half goes, an assertion that is merely a clause inside it goes with it, and the mode contract silently stops being checked.

Extracting it first is what prevents that. While the byte comparison is still effective, the mode check becomes an assertion in its own right, reading the declarations and the repository modes directly. From then on the contract is guarded continuously — there is no revision in which one guard has been retired and its replacement has not yet landed. Doing it in the other order would leave exactly such a gap, and a permission change during that window would go unreported.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A standalone assertion checks each declared live asset's executable declaration against the mode of the repository file it is drawn from.
- [hard] REQ-02: The assertion is independent of the byte comparison it currently shares a loop with, so retiring that comparison leaves it intact.
- [hard] REQ-03: A permission change on a live source alone fails the suite.
- [hard] REQ-04: A declaration claiming an executable file that is not executable fails, and so does the reverse.
- [hard] REQ-05: The assertion is effective from the revision it lands in, while the existing comparison is still effective, so the contract is never unguarded between the two.

## Notes

The assertion is written against the declarations and the repository tree, not against a list of the seven assets that carry the flag today, so a newly declared executable asset is covered without an edit here.

planning.outcome: A standalone assertion checks each declared live asset's executable flag against its repository file's mode.

terminal.test_boundary: in-crate assertions over declared asset modes
terminal.worker_sized_reason: One assertion is lifted out of the loop it shares with a byte comparison, leaving both effective at once.

title: How jit's own workflow profile leaves the binary
description:
How jit's own workflow profile leaves the binary and reaches a repository the way any contributed profile would is established with evidence, so the direction can be executed rather than debated.

## Background

The `jit-dogfood` profile exists today only as bytes compiled into the binary: `crates/jit/src/profile/dogfood.rs` embeds the whole `profiles/jit-dogfood/` directory with `include_dir!` at compile time, and `ProfileOrigin` declares exactly one variant, `Embedded`. There is no discovery of a profile from disk anywhere in the codebase, so a profile cannot presently exist except by being built into the executable that applies it.

Four consumers other than `jit profile apply` read the embedded package, and each is a constraint on the answer: the planning-bracket gate presets, the enumeration of planning gate keys, the profiled initialization path, and derived-state repair.

The owner has ruled the direction. Domain agnosticism is the durable long-term invariant, and binding a specific profile or workflow to the source is a defect rather than a trade-off. The template *system* is engine capability and belongs in the source; a specific application of it — the planning bracket — does not. `@/invariant/domain-agnostic` presently carves the planning-bracket preset trio out as its one sanctioned exception, "retained as the single binary-shipped preset bundle"; that carve-out is what the ruling removes. `@/charter/D-3` decided the plan-before-fan-out workflow itself, which is not in question; only where it lives is.

This is therefore not an open question about whether, and the investigation is not to re-open it. It is an investigation into mechanism and consequence: what a contributed profile is in this codebase, what has to exist for one to be discovered and applied, and what breaks on the way.

The stakes are immediate in two directions. Epic e204e63d's largest story derives the packaged asset tree at build time and makes roughly sixty live repository files inputs to the binary — tightening the coupling the ruling removes; its remaining tasks are halted pending this report. And this project plans every container with `jit apply plan`, whose gates come from the embedded package, so the transition has to keep the repository able to plan its own work.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The mechanism by which the profile reaches a repository today is stated end to end, from the checked-in directory to an applied repository, naming every consumer of the embedded package and what each would lose without it.
- [hard] REQ-02: What a contributed profile is in this codebase is defined concretely: where it lives, how a binary discovers it, how version compatibility and package validation are established for it, and which existing types, wire formats, and code paths already generalize to it rather than needing replacement.
- [hard] REQ-03: The route by which the planning bracket ceases to be binary-shipped content is established, including what an adopter running `jit apply plan` in a fresh repository experiences afterwards and how they obtain the bracket.
- [hard] REQ-04: The amendments the ruling requires are stated in the words they would need: what `@/invariant/domain-agnostic` says once its sanctioned exception is removed, and what if anything `@/charter/D-3` needs, given that the decision it records stands and only the location of its implementation changes.
- [hard] REQ-05: The transition is sequenced so this repository can plan its own containers throughout it, with the step at which `jit apply plan` would otherwise break identified and the ordering that avoids it stated.
- [hard] REQ-06: What remains in the source is separated from what leaves, by principle rather than by enumeration: the criterion distinguishing engine capability from a specific application of it is stated and applied to every consumer found under REQ-01.
- [hard] REQ-07: The effect on each of the following is traced: `jit init`, derived-state repair, package validation, the build-footprint budget, adopter out-of-the-box behaviour, and this repository's own gate registry.
- [hard] REQ-08: The consequences for epic e204e63d's halted work are stated per criterion: which of REQ-03 through REQ-06 survive unchanged, which are superseded, and which become meaningless.
- [hard] REQ-09: The relationship to `@/charter/D-8` is stated, distinguishing what fits inside the deferred profile lifecycle from what reopens it, and if the ruling reopens it that is said plainly rather than absorbed silently.
- [hard] REQ-10: Where genuine alternatives remain inside the ruled direction — the discovery mechanism, the distribution format, the sequencing — each is presented with trade-offs and a recommendation.
- [hard] REQ-11: Every claim about current behaviour carries a file-and-line citation, and no claim rests on inference where the code could be read.

## Non-goals

Implementing any of it. Editing the invariant registry, the charter, or any issue. Re-arguing the direction: the owner has ruled, and evidence that the transition is costly is a finding about cost and sequencing, not grounds to recommend against it.

## Notes

The two projection stories of epic e204e63d (`25bdda50`, `6f8f02ba`) and the convergence task `65ff0f38` continue independently and are not blocked by this.

Owner ruling (2026-07-31): "Domain agnosticism is the only durable long-term invariant. Tying specific profiles and workflows to the source is bad practice. Template system, for instance, belongs to source, but specific applications like the planning bracket do not." This supersedes the issue's original framing, which treated a binary-shipped bracket as a live option.

planning.outcome: One report establishes the mechanism, the ordering, and the consequences of taking the profile out of the binary.

terminal.test_boundary: the report's per-claim citation of the code it describes
terminal.worker_sized_reason: One investigation over one subsystem, answering the questions the ruling opened.

title: Validation stops loading a profile package unconditionally
description:
Whole-repository validation stops depending on one workflow's bytes, so a repository that has applied no profile validates and repairs without any profile package being loaded.

## Background

Repository validation and derived-state repair each load a profile package before doing anything else, unconditionally and by a compiled-in identity, and propagate the failure if that load does not succeed. Every repository pays this, including one that has never applied a profile and never will.

The dependency is invisible today because the package is compiled into the binary and therefore always loads. It stops being invisible the moment the package is no longer carried in the binary: validation would then fail in every repository, including repositories with no profile, and the gates that certify this project's own work run that same command. That makes this the one step whose ordering is not a preference — everything else in the profile extraction is blocked behind it.

The repository already records what it has applied. Applying a profile writes a provenance record under the tracker's own data root, named for the profile it records, and repair compares the repository's state against what that profile's package declares. So the question "is a package needed here, and which one" has an answer in the repository rather than in the binary, and reading it there is what removes the compiled-in dependency.

Two behaviours have to survive the change. A repository with an applied profile must still have its profile-owned targets repaired, which is the capability `@/invariant/derived-state-coherence` rests on. And a repository whose record names a profile whose package cannot be produced must say so rather than proceed: repairing only the targets it can still account for would silently narrow what repair means, which is the failure mode worth designing against now rather than discovering later.

This change removes an unconditional dependency. It does not add profile discovery, does not change where a package comes from, and does not remove the package from the binary — each of those is separate work that this unblocks.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A repository that has applied no profile completes whole-repository validation without any profile package being loaded, and completes derived-state repair the same way.
- [hard] REQ-02: A repository that has applied a profile still has its profile-owned targets checked and repaired exactly as before, with no change to what repair reports or restores.
- [hard] REQ-03: Whether a package is required, and which one, is decided from the repository's own applied-profile record rather than from an identity compiled into the binary.
- [hard] REQ-04: A repository whose record names a profile whose package cannot be obtained reports that condition plainly and fails rather than repairing the subset it can still account for.
- [hard] REQ-05: Repository validation that has nothing to do with profiles behaves identically in all three cases above.
- [hard] REQ-06: Each of the three cases — no record, a record whose package resolves, a record whose package does not — is covered by a test that distinguishes it from the other two.

## Non-goals

Adding discovery of a package from disk. Changing where a package comes from. Removing the package from the binary. Touching the planning-bracket gate presets. Each is separate work that this issue unblocks and does not perform.

## Notes

The two call sites are the repository-validation path and the derived-state-repair path in the validation command; both take the package before opening their mutation session.

Owner-ruled context (2026-07-31): jit's own workflow profile is to leave the binary and be consumed the way an externally contributed profile is (`@/invariant/domain-agnostic`, whose sanctioned exception the ruling removes). This issue is the first step of that route and the only one with a strict ordering constraint: taken after the package leaves the binary instead of before, validation fails in every repository and the gates that would certify the change fail with it.

planning.outcome: Validation resolves a profile package only where the repository's own record names one.

terminal.test_boundary: in-crate repair-plan assertions over the recorded case beside the unrecorded one
terminal.worker_sized_reason: One load moves behind the repository's own record, in the one command that performed it unconditionally.

title: Relocate the packaged gate machinery out of the script directory
description:
The packaged gate machinery this repository keeps under its script directory moves into the contributed-gate directory, and the two byte-identical copies of the review wrapper become one, so every declared live-source root is a directory where packaging is the rule rather than the exception.

## Background

Five live assets are drawn from the script directory: the AI-review wrapper and three review prompts. Forty-one other tracked files there are not packaged, and no category separates the two groups — `code-review-prompt.md` and `plan-review-prompt.md` are packaged while `doc-review-prompt.md` and `holistic-review-prompt.md`, files of exactly the same shape and purpose, are not.

That makes the script directory unusable as a completeness-checked root. Exclusions there could only be a list of forty-one near-literals, which is the hand-maintained inventory the completeness check exists to remove; and every script added later for unrelated reasons would fail the suite until someone added an entry for it. The other roots do not have this problem: the skill tree's unpackaged files are evaluation harnesses, fixtures, transcripts and trigger records, all of which a handful of category patterns cover.

The wrapper is also carried twice. `scripts/ai-review.sh` and `contrib/gates/ai-review.sh` are byte-identical, both declared as packaged assets with different targets, so an adopter installing the package receives two copies of one script. One test exercises both, and a prior container had to fix the same parser defect in each. This is a third duplicate pair of exactly the kind the container removes, sitting inside the inventory the container derives.

Moving the four to the contributed-gate directory makes packaging the rule in every declared root and retires the script directory as one. The contributed-gate directory's own unpackaged material — the README and the example prompts beneath it — is a category a single pattern describes.

The move is a relocation, not a rewrite: the same scripts, the same prompt text, the same behaviour. What changes is where they live in this repository, where an adopter receives them, and the paths that name them.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The AI-review wrapper and the three packaged review prompts live under the contributed-gate directory, and no packaged live asset is drawn from the script directory.
- [hard] REQ-02: One copy of the AI-review wrapper remains in the repository and one packaged asset declares it; the retired copy is gone rather than left behind unreferenced.
- [hard] REQ-03: Every gate in this repository's registry that invoked the wrapper or named one of the moved prompts resolves to the relocated path, and each such gate still evaluates.

title: Regenerating a checked-in generated artifact has one invocation form
description:
Regenerating a generated artifact that lives in the checkout is invoked the same way for every such artifact, so the repository carries one form of this operation rather than two.

## Background

Several files in this repository are generated into the working tree and committed: reference documents rendered from engine declarations, and marked regions rendered from a packaged authority. Each has an assertion that fails when the committed bytes drift from what its source now renders, and each needs a way for a contributor to bring the committed bytes back into agreement.

Two shapes of that second half now exist. Six generators are `#[ignore]`d tests beside their asserting sibling, regenerated by naming the ignored test on a cargo command line, or in one case by setting an environment variable while running the assertion itself: `crates/jit/src/gate_presets/reference.rs`, `crates/jit/src/runtime_defaults.rs`, `crates/jit/src/domain/event_catalog.rs`, `crates/jit/src/output.rs`, `crates/jit/src/storage/reference.rs`, and `crates/jit/src/schema.rs`. Two generators added by this container are shell entry points under the script directory, each taking no arguments, printing what it did, and distinguishing "already current" from "refused or could not run" by exit status.

Both shapes satisfy the property that matters most — neither writes during a default test run — so this is not a correctness gap. It is a single operation with two interfaces, which `@/invariant/convention-convergence` names as a defect rather than a matter of taste: a contributor who learns one shape does not thereby know how to regenerate anything using the other, and a reviewer cannot tell from a call site which applies.

The shell entry point is the form to converge on, and the reason is reach rather than preference. It is the only shape available to a generator whose values come from running a built binary rather than from calling library code, which is why this container's documentation-region generator has it; a generator expressed only as an ignored test could not be written that way at all. It also names itself: a directory listing of the script directory enumerates what can be regenerated, where the ignored tests are discoverable only by knowing they exist.

What sits behind the entry point stays free. One generator runs an installed binary against a throwaway directory; another compiles the crate and runs a program that calls the render directly. That difference follows from where each artifact's authority lives and is not part of the convention.

Two constraints bound how this is done. The build-footprint budget counts integration-test targets against a ceiling with one slot free, and sums the bytes of executables built with the test profile; a migration that adds one compiled target per generator spends footprint for no gain, so the target count this adds is a design decision to make deliberately rather than a consequence to discover. And every asserting sibling must survive the migration unweakened — the assertion is what makes drift visible, and the entry point only repairs it.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: Every generated artifact that is written into the checkout and committed is regenerated through the same kind of entry point, invoked the same way, with the same convention for reporting that it changed nothing, changed something, or could not run.
- [hard] REQ-02: The six generators presently expressed as ignored tests or as an environment-gated branch of an assertion are reachable through that entry point.
- [hard] REQ-03: No generator writes into the checkout during a default test run, and a full default test run leaves the working tree clean.
- [hard] REQ-04: Every generated artifact retains an assertion that fails when the committed bytes differ from what its source renders, and the failure names the command that regenerates it.
- [hard] REQ-05: The regeneration path and the assertion for a given artifact read one implementation of its render, so the two cannot disagree.
- [hard] REQ-06: The build-footprint budget's integration-target and executable-byte assertions hold, and the number of compiled targets the migration adds is stated with its reasoning rather than left implicit.
- [hard] REQ-07: A contributor can enumerate what this repository can regenerate, and how, from one place.
- [hard] REQ-08: A regeneration run immediately following a first one reports that it changed nothing, for every artifact.

## Notes

Preserving each generated artifact's byte content is the measure of a correct migration: this changes how regeneration is invoked, not what any generator produces. A migrated generator that alters its output has a defect, whichever side is wrong.

Publication that stages a file and renames it must carry the destination's existing permissions onto the staged file. A temporary file is created owner-only, and git does not track that bit, so a generator that skips this leaves a mode change no diff reveals.

Owner-directed addition (2026-07-31, execution-lead escalation): the container's own work introduced the second shape, and the owner ruled that convergence is mandatory inside this container rather than deferred to a tracked follow-up, so `@/invariant/convention-convergence` holds without an exception.

planning.outcome: A generated artifact committed to this checkout is regenerated through one invocation form.

terminal.test_boundary: the entry points' own self-test over their reported outcomes
terminal.worker_sized_reason: One declaration of the artifact set plus the entry point shape its members already almost shared.

title: Inventory the binary's declarative configuration and sequence its removal
description:
Every site in the binary that carries declarative configuration is inventoried against the boundary in `@/issue/e204e63d/decision/D-13`, and the removal of the whole set is sequenced with evidence, so it can be executed rather than debated.

## Background

`@/invariant/domain-agnostic` says the binary ships the mechanisms that interpret repository configuration and no instance of that configuration. `@/issue/e204e63d/decision/D-13` fixes the boundary at its strictest reading: no type name, label namespace, item kind, documentation-area classification, or workflow rule reaches an adopter compiled into the executable that applies it, whether it names this repository or is generically opinionated. Only mechanism, and defaults for mechanism parameters (`@/issue/e204e63d/decision/D-12`), remain.

A grep-assembled survey found eight sites and is not a basis for sequencing a change of this size. `crates/jit/src/profile/dogfood.rs` and the planning preset trio are already scoped for extraction by this epic. Beyond them the survey reached `SHIPPED_DOCUMENTATION_POLICY` (`crates/jit/src/config.rs:488`), which carries this repository's own development-area names and is what `jit init` scaffolds into an adopter's `[documentation]` table; `GENERATED_ARTIFACTS` (`crates/jit/src/generated_artifacts.rs:80`), which names this repository's generator scripts and documentation targets; the git hook scripts embedded by `crates/jit/src/commands/hooks.rs:7-8`; the configuration template `jit init` writes, declaring a type hierarchy, a namespace registry, and six item kinds; the seeded rules produced by `crates/jit/src/repository_state/default_rules.rs`; and the item-kind defaults at `crates/jit/src/domain/item.rs:55-64`. The survey is a starting point and is not authoritative: it did not distinguish a site that is one instance of a mechanism from a site that is the mechanism, and it did not look for sites that carry configuration without a constant to grep for.

Investigation `a62d444d` (`dev/active/a62d444d/findings.md`) established the mechanism, ordering, and consequences for the profile alone. Its §5.3 gives a five-step ordering whose steps 2 through 5 are unexecuted. This work extends that ordering rather than running beside it.

Six owner decisions bind this work and are not open: `@/issue/e204e63d/decision/D-13` (the boundary), `D-14` (two packages, `jit-dogfood` declaring a dependency on `jit-default`), `D-15` (REQ-01's authority moves to the packaged declaration), `D-16` (both packages ride in the release archive), `D-17` (the registry-derived rules stay, `orphan-leaf` and `strategic-consistency` move), and `D-18` (this audit blocks fan-out).

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: Every site in `crates/` carrying declarative configuration is inventoried with a file-and-line citation, each classified against D-13's boundary as an instance that leaves or a mechanism that stays, with the reason stated in the boundary's own terms. The inventory is established by reading the code rather than by extending the survey above, and a site the survey named but the reading rejects is reported as such.
- [hard] REQ-02: For each site that leaves, its destination is stated: `jit-default`, `jit-dogfood`, or deletion, with the reason. For each site that stays, what makes it a mechanism rather than an instance is stated in a form a reviewer can test.
- [hard] REQ-03: The composition mechanism D-14 requires is specified concretely — how a package declares its dependency on another, how application orders two packages, what happens when both declare the same key with different content, and how the provenance record and the applied-record wire shape represent a composed application. What already generalizes is separated from what must be built, each with a citation.
- [hard] REQ-04: `jit init`'s resulting shape is established: what a bare invocation writes, how `--profile <id> --from <path>` resolves and applies, what becomes of the present scaffold code path, and what an adopter does between unpacking a release archive and creating a first issue.
- [hard] REQ-05: The removal is sequenced as one ordering that extends `a62d444d` §5.3 rather than a second plan beside it. Every strict constraint is stated as an edge with the failure that makes it one, and every step that is indivisible is identified with the evidence for its indivisibility.
- [hard] REQ-06: The consequences for this epic's delivered work are stated per criterion, including REQ-01's retarget under D-15 and any other completed child whose result the removal invalidates, naming the issue and what specifically stops holding.
- [hard] REQ-07: The release-archive change D-16 requires is specified against the current release workflow and release-policy documentation, with its relationship to `@/charter/D-16` stated and any adopter-facing promise it breaks named.
- [hard] REQ-08: Costs with no route back are stated before execution: for each, the step at which the property disappears and the decision that must be taken at that step to preserve or deliberately drop it.
- [hard] REQ-09: Every claim about current behaviour carries a file-and-line citation, and no claim rests on inference where the code could be read.

## Non-goals

Implementing any of it. Editing the invariant registry, the charter, `.jit/` configuration, or any issue. Re-arguing the direction or any of the six binding decisions: evidence that a step is costly is a finding about cost and sequencing, not grounds to recommend against it.

## Notes

The report goes in this issue's artifact directory and is linked to the issue. `dev/active/a62d444d/findings.md` is the precedent for shape and depth, and its section-numbered citation form is reused so this epic's plan can address both reports the same way.

Fan-out on the widened scope blocks on this report (`@/issue/e204e63d/decision/D-18`). The extraction interior that `a62d444d` already sequenced is planned in the same pass, so the sequencing under REQ-05 must be usable as one manifest rather than two.

planning.outcome: Each site in the binary carrying declarative configuration is classified against the boundary and its removal sequenced.

title: Move the package-authored region source out of the derived prefix
description:
The package-authored managed-region source moves out of the prefix that marks files mirroring a repository counterpart, so that prefix denotes exactly one relationship.

## Background

The packaged tree uses a source-path prefix to mark the files it carries that also exist at working paths in this repository. Sixty-one assets sit under it and each has a repository counterpart. One file does not: the managed-region source. Its counterpart is a marked region inside a repository document, not a whole file, so nothing in the repository can be copied to produce it — it is authored inside the package.

While the packaged tree is checked in, the mismatch is only untidy. It stops being untidy as soon as anything reads that prefix as a rule. A step that produces the packaged tree by drawing each prefixed file from its repository counterpart finds no counterpart for this one and has nothing to copy; a step that reconciles the prefix against the set of files it should contain sees a file it cannot account for and removes it. Either way the region source is the single element that makes the rule false, so it has to move before any such rule exists rather than after.

Moving it is a relocation inside the package plus the declared source path that names it. Nothing about the region it produces changes: the same repository document, the same marker identity, the same placement.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The managed-region source sits outside the prefix reserved for package files drawn from a repository counterpart.
- [hard] REQ-02: The manifest names the relocated source, and the region it declares resolves to the same repository target under the same marker identity with the same placement.
- [hard] REQ-03: The existing comparison between the packaged region body and the repository region body passes unchanged after the move.
- [hard] REQ-04: No file remains under the reserved prefix without a repository counterpart, so every path beneath it denotes the same relationship.

## Notes

The relocation is complete on its own and leaves the packaged content an adopter receives identical; only a source path inside the package changes.

planning.outcome: The managed-region source sits outside the prefix reserved for files drawn from repository counterparts.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: One file moves and one declared source path follows it, with the existing region comparison proving the move.

title: Declare the repository roots the packaged live assets are drawn from
description:
The package manifest states which repository roots its live assets are drawn from, so the set anything else has to walk or watch is declared data rather than a fact inferred from an inventory.

## Background

The packaged live assets are drawn from a small number of repository roots: the agent skill tree, the contributed-gate directory, and the tracker's reference directory. Nothing says so. The information exists only implicitly, in the shape of sixty declared asset paths, so anything needing the root set — a build step deciding which directories to watch, a check asking whether every live consumer was packaged — has to infer it or restate it.

The roots are not usable as bare directories. Fifty-two files under the skill tree and four under the contributed-gate directory are deliberately not packaged: evaluation harnesses, fixtures, transcripts, trigger records, and contributed example prompts. A literal list of those paths would itself be a hand-maintained inventory that goes stale, so exclusions are patterns rather than path literals, and each pattern describes a category rather than a file.

Unknown keys are rejected where the manifest is parsed, so the declaration has to be additive: a manifest without it still parses, and no existing key changes meaning. Keeping the declaration in the manifest rather than in engine code also keeps a repository-local fact inside the package where it belongs.

Roots and patterns are constrained tokens rather than free strings: a malformed entry is rejected at parse time, not discovered later by whatever consumes it. Rejecting a malformed pattern there means compiling it there, so the pattern matcher this work needs is introduced by the type that owns pattern validity rather than by whichever consumer happens to match first.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The manifest declares one entry per repository root the packaged live assets are drawn from, each carrying its own exclusion-pattern list; a list may be empty, since what belongs in it is measured elsewhere.
- [hard] REQ-02: A root and an exclusion pattern are constrained types rejected at parse time when malformed, rather than strings passed through untouched.
- [hard] REQ-03: The addition is additive: a manifest carrying no such declaration still parses, and no existing key changes meaning.
- [hard] REQ-04: The declaration is carried in the value the package's machine-readable inspection output reports.
- [hard] REQ-05: Every repository root the packaged live assets are drawn from is declared, and every live asset's target falls under exactly one declared root.
- [hard] REQ-06: The managed-region source and every install-only asset source fall outside every declared root, so no root claims a package-authored file as a live consumer.

## Notes

Populating the exclusion lists is measurement work: only a walk over the roots can tell whether a pattern set is sufficient, so the lists are filled by the work that performs that walk.

One install-only asset's target path lies inside a declared root, unlike its source. It is absent from this repository, which projects that content elsewhere, so the walk does not meet it here; where it does appear it is unpackaged material like any other and a declared exclusion covers it.

planning.outcome: The package manifest declares each live-source root with the exclusion patterns that bound it.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: One additive declaration on an existing wire type, carrying the roots it describes.

title: Assemble the packaged tree from the repository files it mirrors
description:
One entry point produces the complete package tree from the checked-in package sources and the repository files the manifest's live assets name, and the result is proven equal to the checked-in copies it will replace.

## Background

The package is a directory: a manifest, the assets it declares, and a managed-region source. Sixty of those assets name a repository file as their target and carry a byte copy of it as their source. Producing them instead of carrying them is what removes the second copy, and it is the piece everything else here waits on.

The production does not run in the build. Nothing compiles the package in any more, so a build step would make every build do work no build consumes, and it would reintroduce the directory watching that once relinked every test target on an unchanged rebuild. It runs as a repository entry point over a render inside the crate, which is the shape this repository already uses for the artifacts it generates into its own checkout. That also leaves one reader of the manifest — the crate's own package model — where a build step could only have been a second one, because a build script cannot import the crate it builds.

The destination is disposable. Each run publishes a freshly staged tree, so the result holds exactly what the manifest declares and a source the manifest stops declaring cannot survive into the next run. No incremental reconciliation and no timestamp discipline is needed, and neither is a watch set.

The checked-in copies are still in place while this lands, and that is the point: with both trees present, the produced tree can be compared against the one it will replace, file for file. That comparison is a direct observation rather than a claim made after the originals are gone, and it is the evidence the later retirement rests on.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: One entry point produces the complete package tree at a destination it is given, from the checked-in package sources and the repository files the manifest's live assets name.
- [hard] REQ-02: The render it runs lives in the crate and reads the manifest through the crate's own package model, so nothing parses the manifest a second time.
- [hard] REQ-03: A declared live source whose repository file is absent fails the run with a message naming the path.
- [hard] REQ-04: Each run publishes a freshly staged tree, so a package-relative path the manifest no longer declares is absent from the result.
- [hard] REQ-05: The produced tree carries the same package-relative paths as the checked-in one, with the same bytes and the same executable declaration, and a comparison observes that while both exist.
- [hard] REQ-06: The produced tree validates as a package, so every declared source is present and no produced file is undeclared.
- [hard] REQ-07: The destination is untracked and disposable, and no build depends on it.

## Notes

Where the produced tree goes when it is published is decided by the work that publishes it; this entry point takes a destination and writes there.

planning.outcome: One entry point produces a complete package tree from the checked-in package sources and the repository's live files.

terminal.test_boundary: an in-crate comparison of the assembled tree against the checked-in one
terminal.worker_sized_reason: One render plus its entry point, proven by comparing its output against the tree still checked in beside it.

title: Two assemblies of the package report the same hashes
description:
Two assemblies from the same repository state produce the same package content and report the same content address, so the artefact an adopter receives does not depend on which run produced it.

## Background

Once the packaged tree is produced rather than carried, the artefact an adopter receives is whatever the last assembly wrote. A run that ordered its walk by directory iteration, that embedded a path varying by machine, or that carried a timestamp would produce a different package from the same inputs, and nothing downstream would notice: publication archives whatever it is handed, and the provenance record records whatever digest it is given.

The package model already computes a content address over the canonical manifest and every declared path, plus one digest per installed target. Those are the values an applied-profile record carries, so they are exactly the ones that have to be stable: two repositories installing the same published package must record the same provenance, and a repository validating its own installation must recompute the same digests.

The comparison is between two assemblies into two destinations, never between an assembly and a stored constant. A stored expected digest would be a hand-maintained copy of a derived value and would have to change on every legitimate content edit.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: Two assemblies from the same repository state into two destinations produce the same set of package-relative paths, with identical bytes at each.
- [hard] REQ-02: The package each assembly produces reports the same package hash.
- [hard] REQ-03: The package each assembly produces reports the same per-target digests.
- [hard] REQ-04: Both sides of the comparison are derived from the assemblies the check runs; no expected digest is stored beside it.
- [hard] REQ-05: A content change to a declared live source changes the reported package hash, so the comparison cannot pass by comparing two empty results.

## Notes

The property is about the assembly. Producing byte-identical compiled binaries is a separate concern this work does not scope.

planning.outcome: Two assemblies from identical sources report the same package hash and the same target digests.

terminal.test_boundary: an in-crate comparison of two assemblies
terminal.worker_sized_reason: One check assembles twice into temporary destinations and compares digests the package model already computes.

title: Retire the checked-in copies of the packaged live assets
description:
The sixty packaged files that duplicate repository files exist once, at their working paths, and the assembly is their only producer.

## Background

Each of those files is carried twice: once where this repository consumes it, and once inside the package directory. A test holds the two equal, so drift fails rather than ships, but both copies are hand-maintained and keeping them equal is a step every contributor has to remember. The assembly that precedes this work produces the packaged side from the working side, and its output has already been compared against the checked-in copies file for file, so the second copy has no remaining reason to exist.

Retiring it retires the equality assertion with it, because there is no longer a second copy to compare. Two things must not be lost with it. The executable-mode contract was asserted inside that same comparison loop; it now has a guard of its own, which stays and keeps holding each declared asset's mode against its repository file. And the correspondence between the manifest and the tree stays with the package model, which rejects a declared source that is absent and a package file no declaration claims — so an assembled package still proves it carries exactly what it declares.

What remains checked in is the package's own material: the manifest, the install-only assets, and the managed-region source. Nothing beneath the live-source prefix remains, so that prefix becomes a package-internal namespace the assembly fills rather than a directory anyone edits.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The repository carries no file beneath the package's live-source prefix; every such package-relative path exists only inside an assembled package.
- [hard] REQ-02: The assertion comparing a packaged copy against its repository counterpart is gone, along with the copies it compared.
- [hard] REQ-03: The executable-mode guard still holds each declared live asset's mode against its repository file.
- [hard] REQ-04: An assembled package validates as a package: every declared source resolves and no produced file is undeclared.
- [hard] REQ-05: The checked-in package directory holds the manifest, the install-only assets, and the managed-region source, and nothing drawn from a repository counterpart.

## Notes

Applying the profile from this repository's checkout now means assembling it first. Nothing in this repository applies its own profile, so that costs nothing here; what an adopter receives is the assembled tree, not this directory.

planning.outcome: The packaged live assets exist once in the repository, at their working paths.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: Sixty files are removed and one assertion is retired, against an assembly already proven equal to them.

title: Adjust the citation checker's package exclusions
description:
The citation checker's package exclusions describe the package directory as it exists once the derived prefix is gone, so the check neither scans content it should skip nor skips content it should scan.

## Background

The citation checker scans source paths and qualified item references and reports ones that do not resolve. It carries an exclusion for package content, written when the package directory held both install-only assets and a large tree of copies of repository files. That tree is no longer in the repository, so what the exclusion covers, and what it was protecting against, have both changed.

The question is small but real: an exclusion that was correct against a directory of sixty-odd copied files may be over-broad or under-broad against what remains, which is the install-only assets, the manifest, and the package-authored region source. Leaving it unexamined means the checker's behaviour over package content is determined by a pattern nobody re-read after the thing it described changed shape.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The exclusion describes the package directory as it exists after the derived prefix is gone, covering neither more nor less than intended.
- [hard] REQ-02: The intent the exclusion serves is stated where the pattern lives, so a later reader can judge it against the directory rather than guess.
- [hard] REQ-03: The mechanical documentation checks pass over the adopter surface with the adjusted exclusion.
- [hard] REQ-04: A qualified reference inside the remaining package content resolves or is reported, according to the stated intent.

planning.outcome: The citation checker's package exclusions describe the package directory that remains.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: One exclusion pattern is re-derived against a package directory that no longer holds the derived prefix.

title: Fail on a repository file under a declared root that no packaged asset claims
description:
A repository file beneath a declared live-source root that is neither a packaged asset nor matched by a declared exclusion fails the suite, so a new live consumer cannot be left out of adopter installs unnoticed.

## Background

The existing drift assertion walks one direction only. For each declared asset it reads the repository file it mirrors and compares bytes; nothing enumerates repository files and asks whether each was declared. A new consumer added under a packaged root is therefore absent from every adopter install with nothing reporting it, and the nearest existing guard is a hand-written four-path spot check — a sample, and itself a hand-maintained list.

The reverse direction is already closed inside the package: package validation rejects a file present in the package directory that the manifest does not declare. That says nothing about the repository tree, which is the gap here.

Two properties shape the walk. Exclusions have to be patterns, because the non-packaged material under the declared roots runs to dozens of files — evaluation harnesses, fixtures, transcripts, this repository's own scripts, review prompts — and enumerating them as literals reproduces the hand-maintained inventory the check exists to eliminate. And the walk has to consider only files the repository tracks, so a contributor's scratch file under a packaged root is not reported as a packaging defect; a run that cannot obtain that listing has to fail rather than pass on an empty set.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A test walks each declared live-source root and reports a file that is neither a declared packaged asset nor matched by a declared exclusion.
- [hard] REQ-02: The report names the offending path, so the reader can decide between packaging it and excluding it.
- [hard] REQ-03: Exclusion patterns are globs matched against repository-relative paths, so a directory of unpackaged material costs one entry rather than one per file.
- [hard] REQ-04: The declared exclusions cover the unpackaged material present under those roots today, and the test passes against the current tree.
- [hard] REQ-05: An unpackaged file added under a declared root that no exclusion matches fails the test.
- [hard] REQ-06: The walk considers only paths the repository tracks, and a run that cannot obtain that listing fails rather than passing on an empty set.
- [hard] REQ-07: Every packaged live asset is covered by some declared root, so no packaged file escapes the check.

## Notes

Exclusion patterns are chosen to describe categories of material rather than individual files, so that a further evaluation harness or review prompt of the same shape needs no new entry. The script root is the case where this matters most: it already holds this repository's own documentation-generation and check scripts, more of them are being written in parallel with this work, and a pattern covering that category keeps the declaration correct whichever order those land in.

The workspace's established repository-inventory idiom lists untracked non-ignored paths alongside tracked ones, which is the opposite of the property this walk needs. Copying that flag set would report a contributor's scratch file as a packaging defect; the listing here is the tracked-only one.

The pattern matcher is already available through the type that validates the declared patterns, so this work adds no dependency of its own.

planning.outcome: An undeclared, unexcluded file under a declared live-source root fails the suite.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: One walk over four declared roots, plus the exclusion patterns that make it pass today.

title: Cover the declared roots on the agent-facing bridge
description:
The bridge that exposes profile inspection to agents is covered for the root declaration, so an additive manifest change is observed on that surface rather than assumed compatible with it.

## Background

The profile manifest's shape is public twice over: once through the command-line inspection output, and once through the bridge that republishes the same command surface to agent clients. The bridge's own suite drives the profile inspection tool against this package and asserts on the manifest it gets back, which is what makes it a real consumer rather than a pass-through nobody checks.

A recorded constraint from the work that built this package applies directly: changes must preserve the public profile, schema, and bridge journey rather than silently invalidating it. An additive field satisfies that by construction, but "by construction" is the claim, not the evidence. The evidence is an assertion on the surface itself, in the suite that already exercises it.

The assertion belongs to a different workspace from the type it observes, with its own toolchain and its own suite, which is why it stands apart from the declaration it covers.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The bridge's integration suite asserts that the reported manifest carries the root declaration.

title: State the root declaration in the adopter manifest reference
description:
The adopter reference that describes what the package manifest carries accounts for the declared roots, so its enumeration of the manifest's contents is not silently incomplete.

## Background

The adopter reference for packaged workflows describes the manifest as the package inventory and lists what it holds: version, contributions, assets, managed regions, hashes, and executable declarations. That sentence is a hand-written enumeration of a structure that has just gained a section, which makes it the kind of copy that is wrong the moment its subject changes.

The page's own approach is to point a reader at the inspection command for exact contents rather than reproduce them, which is the right shape and should be kept. What needs saying is that the manifest also declares where the packaged live assets are drawn from — a fact an adopter reading about the package's structure would otherwise not learn exists.

title: The packaged asset tree is derived from the repository files it mirrors
description:
The packaged live-asset tree is produced from the repository files it mirrors rather than carried as a second checked-in copy, and a live consumer that no packaged asset claims fails the suite.

## Background

Sixty of the package's files are byte copies of files this repository also carries at their working paths. A test holds each pair equal, so drift fails rather than ships, but both copies are hand-maintained and the test walks one direction only: it never asks whether a live file that belongs in the package was declared, so a newly added consumer is absent from every adopter install with nothing reporting it.

Both halves close here. One entry point assembles the package from the working files the manifest declares, the duplicated copies retire once the produced tree has been compared against them, and the manifest declares the repository roots its live assets are drawn from so a walk can report a file under any of them that no packaged asset claims and no declared exclusion covers.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The packaged live-asset tree is produced from the repository files it mirrors, and no copy of any of them is checked in.
- [hard] REQ-02: Two assemblies from the same repository state produce identical package content and report identical digests.
- [hard] REQ-03: Every root the packaged live assets are drawn from is declared with the exclusion patterns that bound it.
- [hard] REQ-04: A tracked repository file under a declared root that no packaged asset claims and no declared exclusion covers fails the suite.
- [hard] REQ-05: The adopter-facing description of what the manifest carries accounts for the declaration, and the agent-facing bridge observes it.

## Notes

The produced tree is the artefact the profile's distribution publishes, so this work is the input to taking the profile out of the binary rather than a change beside it.

title: Read a profile package from a directory on disk
description:
A profile package is constructed from a directory tree, owning the bytes it validates, so a package that is not compiled into the binary can exist at all.

## Background

The package model was written as if its bytes were untrusted external data, and almost all of it already holds for a package of unknown provenance: it takes a path-to-bytes map, bounds file count and total size, rejects absolute, traversal, Windows-prefix, control-character and backslash paths, rejects a declared source that is absent and a package file no declaration claims, rejects duplicate sources and duplicate targets, and content-addresses the manifest and every path.

Two things stand in the way. The only constructor that exists walks a directory compiled in at build time. And the type borrows the byte slices it validates, which a disk read cannot supply without leaking them. A directory walk producing a path-to-bytes map, over a representation that can own its bytes, is therefore the entire new reader.

What the reader must not do is relax any defence. A package read from a working tree is exactly the untrusted input those bounds were written for, and a directory entry that is not a regular file, or a path that escapes the package root, has to be rejected where the package is read rather than where its content is used.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A profile package is constructed from a directory path, owning the bytes it validates.
- [hard] REQ-02: For the same content, a directory-read package and a compile-time package are equal in manifest, package hash, and per-target digests.
- [hard] REQ-03: Every existing package defence applies to a directory-read package: the file-count and total-size bounds, the rejected path shapes, the absent declared source, and the undeclared package file.
- [hard] REQ-04: A directory entry that is not a regular file, and any path escaping the package root, is rejected with a message naming it.
- [hard] REQ-05: A directory that is absent or unreadable is reported as such rather than as an invalid package.

## Notes

Where a package directory comes from is decided elsewhere. This is the reader alone.

planning.outcome: A profile package is constructed from a directory tree, owning its bytes rather than borrowing compiled-in ones.

title: Record where an applied package came from
description:
The repository's applied-profile record carries the location the package was read from, so a later run can read the same package again.

## Background

The record beside an applied profile carries its id, its version, its origin, the package's content address, and a digest per installed target. Origin has one value, meaning the bytes were compiled into the binary — a vocabulary shaped for a second one but never given it. So a repository that applied a package from a directory has nowhere to say so, and nothing that runs later has anywhere to look for the bytes.

The location belongs in this record and nowhere else. It is repository-local state, versioned with the repository that applied the profile, and it is the one place that has to agree with itself. Putting the same location in a configuration key as well would create two carriers of one fact and a precedence question between them.

Where the location may point is part of the contract. A location outside the worktree makes a repository's derived-state repair depend on machine state, so the record is confined to a worktree-relative path and an application from outside it is refused rather than recorded.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The applied-profile record carries the repository-relative location the package was read from.
- [hard] REQ-02: The recorded location lies inside the repository worktree; applying a package from outside it is refused, naming the path.
- [hard] REQ-03: The record's origin distinguishes a package read from a repository location from one compiled into the binary.
- [hard] REQ-04: Application records the location it actually read from, not one supplied independently of the bytes.
- [hard] REQ-05: A record whose location is absent or malformed is a validation failure rather than an ignored field.

## Notes

The record carries a path, never package content. No package bytes are written under the tracker's data root.

planning.outcome: The applied-profile record carries the worktree-relative location the package was read from, and its origin.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: One field on a persisted record and one variant on its origin, written where application already builds it.

title: Resolve a profile package from a given location or the repository's record
description:
The profile commands read their package from a location the caller gives or from the location the repository's own record names, so a package that is not compiled in can be inspected, applied, and re-read.

## Background

Resolution today compares a requested id against one compiled-in package and returns it or reports the profile missing, and enumeration returns a one-element list built from that same package. Neither can express a package that lives in a directory, so every profile command is limited to the one the binary carries.

Two routes replace it, in a fixed order. A location the caller gives answers the first application: an adopter who has obtained a package has bytes and no record yet. The location the repository's record names answers every run after that, without the caller having to remember where the package came from. While a package is still compiled in, it stays as the last resort behind both, so nothing that works today stops working before the package it depends on has left.

Enumeration follows the same principle: what the repository reports is what its own records name, each resolved from its recorded location, so the answer describes this repository rather than the binary.

A recorded location that no longer resolves is a failure and says so. Reporting it as an absent profile would make a deleted directory look like a repository that never applied one.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A profile command reads its package from an explicitly given repository location when one is supplied.
- [hard] REQ-02: With no location supplied, a profile command reads the package from the location the repository's applied-profile record names.
- [hard] REQ-03: A supplied location takes precedence over a recorded one, and both take precedence over any package compiled into the binary.
- [hard] REQ-04: Enumeration reports the profiles the repository's own records name, each resolved from its recorded location.
- [hard] REQ-05: A recorded location that no longer resolves is reported as an error naming the record and the path, never as an absent profile.

## Notes

Initialization applying a profile takes the same supplied location, because a repository being created has no record to read.

planning.outcome: The profile commands read a package from a given location or from the location the repository's record names.

What it says is the resolution order, because that is what an adopter needs to predict: a supplied location wins, the location the repository's own record names is used when none is supplied, and a recorded location that no longer resolves is an error rather than an absent profile.
