title: Repair profile-owned targets from the recorded package location
description:
Derived-state repair recomputes a recorded profile's expected targets by reading its package again from the location the record names, and fails loudly when that location no longer resolves.

## Background

Repair works today because the package is always obtainable: the expected record can be recomputed from it and compared against the stored one, and only an exact match yields the claims that restore a deleted or edited profile-owned target. Once the package lives in a directory, "the package is resolvable" and "the binary exists" stop being the same statement, and repair needs somewhere to look.

The record's own location is that place, and it is the only one. The alternative — trusting the stored digests when the package cannot be read — would quietly turn repair from restoring profile-owned targets into restoring the ones it can still account for, which is a regression in the coherence the repair path exists to uphold.

So an unresolvable location is an error that names the record and the path. A repository with no applied-profile record is untouched: it resolves no package and reports nothing about profiles, which is already true and stays true.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: Where a record names a location that resolves, repair recomputes the expected record from the package read there and restores a deleted or edited profile-owned target.
- [hard] REQ-02: Where the recorded location does not resolve, validation fails naming the record and the path.
- [hard] REQ-03: No expected target is ever derived from the stored record's own digests.
- [hard] REQ-04: A repository with no applied-profile record reads no package and reports nothing about profiles.
- [hard] REQ-05: A stored record that disagrees with the package read from the recorded location is a validation failure rather than a repair.

## Notes

This is what keeps the repair guarantee whole once the bytes leave the binary; the location's confinement to the worktree is what keeps it a property of the repository rather than of the machine.

planning.outcome: Repair recomputes a recorded profile's expected targets by re-reading its package from the recorded location.

title: Declare one package's dependency on another
description:
A package manifest states the packages it depends on, so a package can carry a delta over another rather than a copy of it.

## Background

The manifest rejects unknown keys, with the explicit comment that future composition syntax cannot silently enter the v1 contract. A dependency declaration is therefore a deliberate change to that contract rather than an additive field that slips in, and it carries a schema regeneration: the manifest schema is public through the package's machine-readable inspection output and through the agent-facing bridge over it.

The declaration is what makes two packages legitimate. Without it, a package needing another's vocabulary has to restate it, and the two copies are held equal by an assertion — the shape this container exists to remove.

This states the dependency. Resolving and applying one is separate work, so a manifest declaring a dependency parses and reports it here, and acquires its meaning when the resolution that reads it lands.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A package manifest declares the package ids it depends on, and a manifest declaring none parses exactly as it does today.
- [hard] REQ-02: A malformed or self-referential dependency declaration is rejected where the manifest is parsed, naming the offending entry.
- [hard] REQ-03: The declaration is carried in the value the package's machine-readable inspection output reports, and the published manifest schema is regenerated from the changed type.
- [hard] REQ-04: A dependency id is a constrained identifier of the same shape as a package id, rejected at parse time when malformed.

## Notes

Nothing here resolves a dependency or changes what application does; a package that declares one behaves exactly as it does today until the resolution work lands.

planning.outcome: A package manifest declares the package ids it depends on, and the published schema carries the declaration.

title: Give the contribution vocabulary the tables the scaffold writes
description:
A package contributes the documentation-area classification and the validation defaults, so the configuration a repository receives can come from a package rather than from the binary.

## Background

A package's contributions reach the type hierarchy, the label associations, the namespaces, the item kinds, the strategic types, and the three registry files. Two tables the scaffold writes have no target at all: the documentation-area classification, and the validation defaults that carry a strictness and a default type name. A package cannot declare either today, so the configuration that carries them cannot move out of the binary until it can.

Granularity is the design question. The documentation table is five keys, three of them lists. One target carrying the whole table would force any second package that wants one area to restate all five keys — the copy this container exists to remove. Per-key targets let a package declare only what it owns, and two packages collide only where both declare the same key, which is the conflict rule the existing merge already applies.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A package contributes each documentation-area key independently: the two scalar keys as single values, the three list keys as sets.
- [hard] REQ-02: A package contributes the validation strictness and the default type name independently.
- [hard] REQ-03: Two packages declaring the same key with the same content merge to that content; declaring it with different content is the same hard conflict the existing merge raises, with no precedence between them.
- [hard] REQ-04: A repository whose applied packages declare none of these keys receives none of them, and the tables it authored itself are untouched.
- [hard] REQ-05: The additions are carried in the value the package's machine-readable inspection output reports.

## Notes

This adds targets. What any package puts in them is decided by the work that assembles a package.

planning.outcome: A package contributes the documentation-area keys and the validation defaults, one key at a time.

terminal.test_boundary: in-crate contribution merge assertions
terminal.worker_sized_reason: Two tables gain targets on a model that already has six, merged by the rule the existing targets use.

title: Apply a package together with the packages it depends on
description:
Applying a package resolves and applies the packages it declares a dependency on first, so a package carrying a delta over another produces the same repository as one carrying both.

## Background

A dependency declaration means nothing until something reads it. Applying a package that depends on another must resolve the dependency from the same routes the package itself came from, apply it first, and only then apply the dependant — otherwise the dependant's declarations land against a repository missing the vocabulary they extend.

Most of what this needs already exists. Provenance is one record per package id, and validation already lists that directory, derives the recorded ids, and resolves every one of them, so repair over several applied packages needs no change. Contribution merge is idempotent for identical restatements and a hard error otherwise, so two packages compose without a new merge rule. What is missing is the ordering itself, a cycle rejection, and the diagnosis when one package of a set cannot be resolved.

That last one is the sharp edge. A repository that applied a workflow package and then deleted the package it depends on fails validation naming a package the adopter never asked for by name. The error has to explain the relationship, or an adopter is left diagnosing something they never installed.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: Applying a package resolves every package it declares a dependency on, transitively, and applies each before the package that declares it.
- [hard] REQ-02: A dependency cycle is rejected before anything is applied, naming the cycle.
- [hard] REQ-03: Each applied package writes its own provenance record carrying its own hashes, and an application event is appended per package.
- [hard] REQ-04: A dependency that cannot be resolved fails the application before anything is written, naming the package that declared the dependency alongside the one that could not be resolved.
- [hard] REQ-05: Validation reporting an unresolvable recorded package states which recorded package declared it, where one did.
- [hard] REQ-06: Applying a package whose dependencies are already applied and unchanged reports no work.

## Notes

Ordering is a topological sort over declared dependencies. The graph layer already owns that shape; what is new is a caller for it in the profile layer.

planning.outcome: Applying a package applies the packages it depends on first, each with its own record and event.

terminal.test_boundary: command-harness assertions over a composed application
terminal.worker_sized_reason: One topological resolution in front of an application path that already applies one package.

title: Name the declaring package when two packages collide
description:
A conflict between two packages' declarations names both packages, so a collision is diagnosed as a package conflict rather than as adopter drift.

## Background

Two failure paths guard a composed application. A second package declaring a key the first already wrote with different content fails the contribution merge; a second package declaring an asset target the first wrote with different bytes fails the target conflict. Both are the right semantics and stay: a dependant silently overriding its dependency's declarations would give it authority no criterion grants, and validation could not then distinguish an override from drift.

Neither error names the other package. The contribution error carries the identity and the registry; the target error carries the path. Before composition that was complete, because there was only ever one package and the occupant was the adopter's own content. With two, the same message tells an adopter their file conflicts with itself.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A contribution conflict between two packages names both the package whose declaration is already in the image and the package whose declaration conflicts with it.
- [hard] REQ-02: An asset target conflict between two packages names both packages and the target path.
- [hard] REQ-03: A conflict between a package and content the repository authored still reports the repository as the occupant, distinguishably from a package-to-package conflict.
- [hard] REQ-04: The conflict semantics are unchanged: identical restatements merge, differing ones fail, and no package takes precedence over another.

## Notes

This is a message and error-payload change. Nothing about which applications succeed changes.

planning.outcome: A conflict between two packages' declarations names both packages.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: Two error payloads gain the package identity the composition path already holds.

title: A profile package is read from disk, and packages compose
description:
The engine reads, verifies, applies, composes, and repairs profile packages that live in repository directories, so a profile no longer has to be compiled in to exist and a package can carry a delta over another.

## Background

A profile can presently exist only as bytes compiled into the binary: one constructor walks a compiled-in directory, one resolver compares a requested id against one compiled-in package, and the applied-profile record's origin has a single value meaning exactly that. Everything else about the package model already treats its bytes as untrusted external data, and provenance is already one record per package id, so repair over several applied packages needs no change.

What is missing is a reader, somewhere to record where a package came from, a resolver that uses it, a way for one package to declare a dependency on another, and the ordering that applies them. Two tables the configuration needs — the documentation-area classification and the validation defaults — have no contribution target at all, so a package cannot yet carry the configuration a repository receives.

One thing deliberately stays missing. A package declares which jit versions it is written for, and that declaration is parsed and not matched against the running binary; a package built for a later binary applies cleanly and fails wherever the shape later differs. Matching it belongs to the profile lifecycle the charter defers (`@/issue/e204e63d/decision/D-19`).

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A profile package is constructed from a repository directory, with every existing package defence applying to it.
- [hard] REQ-02: The applied-profile record carries the worktree-relative location the package was read from.
- [hard] REQ-03: Profile inspection, application, and initialization read their package from a given location or from the recorded one.
- [hard] REQ-04: A package declares the packages it depends on, and applying it applies those first, each with its own record and event.
- [hard] REQ-05: A package contributes the documentation-area keys and the validation defaults, and a collision between two packages names both.
- [hard] REQ-06: Derived-state repair recomputes expected targets from the package read at the recorded location, and fails loudly when it cannot.

## Notes

Nothing here removes the compiled-in package; it becomes the last resort behind two better answers, and leaves when the work that puts the packages in the release archive has landed.

planning.outcome: The engine reads, applies, composes, and repairs profile packages that live in repository directories.

title: Stop supplying a taxonomy to a repository that declares none
description:
A repository that declares no label namespaces and no type hierarchy receives none, so nothing the adopter did not declare reaches their configuration.

## Background

Three copies of a four-level type hierarchy and one copy of a three-namespace registry live in default implementations and fallback branches, reached whenever the configuration omits the corresponding table. Their effect is measurable rather than theoretical: a repository whose configuration declares neither table is initialized with a rule set naming six namespaces and four type names it never declared, plus two committed JSON schemas enumerating them. Validation passes, so nothing reports it.

The three sites are one property, not three. One of them feeds the namespace rule and its schema, one feeds the type-hierarchy rule through a different caller, and one feeds the graph rules. Any one left behind keeps a compiled taxonomy reachable and the property unobservable.

This also has to land before the configuration the scaffold writes is removed. Deleting that template while these defaults remain makes every default initialization take exactly the route above — the failure would be silent, and it would be caused by the change intended to prevent it.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A repository whose configuration declares no label namespaces receives an empty namespace registry, and no rule or schema enumerating namespaces is written.
- [hard] REQ-02: A repository whose configuration declares no type hierarchy receives no hierarchy, and no rule or schema enumerating type names is written.
- [hard] REQ-03: A repository that declares either table is unaffected, receiving exactly what it declared.
- [hard] REQ-04: The three compiled taxonomy sources are gone, along with the fallback branches that reached them.
- [hard] REQ-05: A repository declaring neither table still validates, and the rule set it receives is the label grammar alone.

## Notes

The rules that project a registry stay: each derives both its assertion and its membership from whatever the adopter declared, and produces nothing when they declared nothing. That property is only observable once these defaults are gone.

planning.outcome: A repository declaring no namespaces and no type hierarchy receives neither.

title: Author a test fixture that declares its own taxonomy

One shared fixture builds a repository whose configuration declares a type hierarchy and the namespaces tests assert on, so no test has to depend on the binary supplying either.

The shared test-utility module is where the crate's suites already reach for repository setup, so it goes there and every other suite consumes it — a fixture per module family would satisfy the sizing of the adoptions while producing the near-duplicate setup the shared-contract rule exists to prevent.

Its vocabulary is the suite's own, chosen for the assertions that read it, and deliberately not a copy of what any package declares: a test asserting that a strategic type resolves is testing the mechanism, not the vocabulary.

- [hard] REQ-04: Its own assertions establish that a repository built through it carries exactly the declared hierarchy and namespaces.

Every adoption entry consumes this fixture as authored. If one needs a different vocabulary, it declares that beside its own assertions rather than adding a second fixture.

## Background

Two things carry this project's workflow inside the binary: the whole package directory, and three gate presets whose names and shapes are read out of it. Both are applications of the mechanisms around them rather than mechanisms, so both leave under one rule.

Removing them is bounded by two facts and one ordering. Nothing an adopter can do today stops working: a gate key resolves through the repository's own registry when no preset supplies it. Nothing this repository does stops working: its own bracket gates are hand-authored and it has never applied its own profile. And the package must ride in the release archive and be provably applicable from it before the compiled-in copy stops existing.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The binary compiles in no profile package and no workflow preset, and the generated preset reference matches what remains.
- [hard] REQ-02: This repository's own tests read the package from its checkout rather than from a compiled-in copy.
- [hard] REQ-03: Editing a packaged source no longer reports an installed binary as stale.
- [hard] REQ-04: No superseded embedded-package name survives, in the crate, the command help, or the agent-facing bridge.

## Notes

The rest of the boundary — the configuration the binary writes, the named bundles, the vocabulary literals, and this checkout's own paths — is delivered beside this rather than inside it.

planning.outcome: The workflow profile and its presets have left the binary, riding in the release archive instead.

description:
The configuration a new repository receives, the named content bundles, the vocabulary literals in every shipped artefact, and this checkout's own paths have all left the binary, and the invariant states the rule that keeps them out.

## Background

Beyond one project's workflow, the binary carries a whole configuration it renders for every new repository, four named icon bundles selectable by name, a label namespace built from a literal in two commands, this repository's own gate keys and item ids in the agent-facing bridge's shipped text, a type hierarchy and a namespace colour table in the web bundle, and the documentation and script paths of this checkout. Each produces content an adopter never declared, so each is an instance rather than a mechanism.

What stays is named as carefully as what goes: the defaults that name a mechanism's own parameter, and the rules that derive both their assertion and their membership from whatever registry the adopter declared. The amended invariant carries both classes explicitly, because a narrower wording would delete the first by implication and be silent where the boundary reaches furthest.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A bare initialization writes the structural minimum, and no compiled configuration template, named hierarchy bundle, or named icon bundle remains.
- [hard] REQ-02: No type name or label namespace literal remains in the engine's own label construction, in the agent-facing bridge's shipped text, or in the web bundle's rendering paths.
- [hard] REQ-03: No path inside this checkout is reachable from an adopter build.
- [hard] REQ-04: The project invariant carries no sanctioned exception and states which names belong to a mechanism, reaching every class the boundary names.
- [hard] REQ-05: The adopter-facing documentation describes obtaining and applying the published packages, the affordance that goes with the removal, and the two workflow warnings a repository stops receiving unless it applies the workflow package.

## Notes

The generated policy regions are repaired inside the change that breaks them, because their generator reads the very table the removal stops writing.

planning.outcome: Every configuration the binary wrote, every named bundle, and every vocabulary literal has left it.
